# Add a second node

<!-- type: tutorial · level: 1 -->

**Needs first:** [What you just built](what-you-just-built.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: chapter status -->

In this chapter you add a listener to the project: a second node package,
`monitor_node`, that subscribes to `/chatter`. At the end, one run of the
board prints both sides of the conversation:

```text
[INFO] sensor_node: [    1.025751] Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
[INFO] monitor_node: [    1.026723] I heard: [Hello World: 1]
```

Along the way you see what makes `sensor_ws` a workspace, and why adding a
node is one package and one line in the bringup.

Run every step from the root of `sensor_ws`.

## Add the listener package

<!-- tabs -->

#### Rust

```bash probe=310 track=installed variant=qemu
nros new monitor_node --template listener --lang rust --to sensor_node_bringup
```

#### C

```bash probe=310 track=installed variant=qemu
nros new monitor_node --template listener --lang c --to sensor_node_bringup
```

#### C++

```bash probe=310 track=installed variant=qemu
nros new monitor_node --template listener --lang cpp --to sensor_node_bringup
```

<!-- /tabs -->

```text
nros new: added the node package src/monitor_node/ (listener, rust) to /home/you/sensor_ws
  declared it in /home/you/sensor_ws/src/sensor_node_bringup: a [[component]] row and an <exec_depend>
```

Inside a workspace, `nros new` adds a package under `src/` instead of writing
a new workspace. `--template listener` picks the node it holds: a
subscription on `/chatter` that prints each message it receives. `--to
sensor_node_bringup` also tells the bringup to run it, which the next step
looks at. Without `--to`, no bringup is touched, and the package sits in the
workspace until a bringup names it.

Use the language of the rest of your project. A workspace can mix languages,
and [Mix languages](../guide/build/mix-languages.md) shows how, but this
Tutorial keeps to one.

## Read the listener

The new package has the shape of `sensor_node`: a library holding one node,
with no `main()` and no board.

<!-- tabs -->

#### Rust

```text
src/monitor_node/
├── Cargo.toml          # a [lib] crate; registers monitor_node::Listener
├── package.xml         # <depend>std_msgs</depend>
└── src/lib.rs          # the listener; its last line is nros::node!(Listener);
```

`register` creates one subscription and binds it to the callback named
`on_chatter`. `on_callback` reads the message when that callback fires:

```rust
fn register(ctx: &mut NodeContext<'_>) -> NodeResult<()> {
    nros_log::register_logger(&LOGGER);
    let mut node = ctx.create_node(NodeOptions::new("monitor_node"))?;
    let _sub =
        node.create_subscription_for_callback_name::<StringMsg>("on_chatter", "/chatter")?;
    log_info!(&LOGGER, "Subscriber created for topic: /chatter");
    Ok(())
}

fn on_callback(state: &mut Self::State, callback: Callback<'_>, ctx: &mut CallbackCtx<'_>) {
    if callback.as_str() == "on_chatter"
        && let Ok(msg) = ctx.message::<StringMsg>()
    {
        *state = state.wrapping_add(1);
        log_info!(&LOGGER, "I heard: [{}]", msg.data);
    }
}
```

`register` declares what the node creates; it does not run the node. It runs
once, at startup, and no message flows during it. `on_callback` is the body,
which the executor calls each time one of the node's callbacks fires;
`state` is the node's own storage, here a count of the messages it has seen.

The constant at the top of the `impl Component` block, `ENTITY_BOUNDS`,
says how many publishers, service servers, service clients, action clients
and action servers the node creates. The talker's is `exact(1, 0, 0, 0, 0)`:
one publisher. The listener's is all zeros, because a subscription needs no
slot there. The numbers size static memory, so they are exact rather than
generous; a node that creates more than it declares stops at boot, naming
the node, rather than dropping one silently.

`Cargo.toml` registers the class the package exports:

```toml
[package.metadata.nros.node]
class = "monitor_node::Listener"
name = "monitor_node"
```

#### C

```text
src/monitor_node/
├── CMakeLists.txt      # registers monitor_node::Listener
├── nros-codegen.toml   # the largest string the node's messages carry
├── package.xml         # <depend>std_msgs</depend>
└── src/Listener.c      # the listener
```

`listener_configure` creates one subscription and adds it to the executor
with a callback and a context pointer, the way rclc does. The message is
owned by the node's state struct, so nothing allocates when one arrives:

```c
static void on_msg(const void* msgin, void* ctx) {
    listener_t* self = (listener_t*)ctx;
    const std_msgs__msg__String* msg = (const std_msgs__msg__String*)msgin;
    printf("I heard: [%.*s]\n", (int)msg->data.size, msg->data.data);
    self->recv++;
}

static rcl_ret_t listener_configure(rcl_node_t* node, rclc_executor_t* executor, listener_t* self) {
    self->recv = 0;
    std_msgs__msg__String__init_in(&self->msg, &self->msg_storage);
    self->sub = rcl_get_zero_initialized_subscription();
    rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_subscription_init_default(
        &self->sub, node, ROSIDL_GET_MSG_TYPE_SUPPORT(std_msgs, msg, String), "/chatter");
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) {
        return rc;
    }
    return rclc_executor_add_subscription_with_context(executor, &self->sub, &self->msg, on_msg,
                                                       self, ON_NEW_DATA);
}

RCLC_C_COMPONENT(listener_t, listener_configure)
```

`std_msgs__msg__String__init_in` points the message's string at
`msg_storage`, memory the node owns. Generated messages take rosidl's C
names and member shape, and their strings and sequences always point at
memory you own: nothing on this path allocates, so rosidl's allocating
`__init` and `__fini` are not declared.

#### C++

```text
src/monitor_node/
├── CMakeLists.txt                     # registers monitor_node::Listener
├── include/monitor_node/Listener.hpp  # the Listener class
├── nros-codegen.toml                  # the largest string the node's messages carry
├── package.xml                        # <depend>std_msgs</depend>
└── src/Listener.cpp                   # its two members
```

`configure` binds the member `on_msg` as the subscription's callback, by
identity rather than through a `std::function`:

```cpp
void Listener::on_msg(const ::std_msgs::msg::String& msg) {
    std::printf("I heard: [%s]\n", msg.data.c_str());
    ++recv_;
}

::rclcpp::Result Listener::configure(::rclcpp::Node& node) {
    return ::rclcpp::bind_subscription<::std_msgs::msg::String, Listener, &Listener::on_msg>(
        node, "/chatter", this);
}
```

Every call returns a `Result` rather than throwing, because every nano-ros
build compiles with `-fno-exceptions`. `configure` returns the first
failure, and the program stops at boot naming the node that failed.
[Port a C++ node](../guide/port/port-a-cpp-node.md) shows the
`rclcpp`-shaped constructors a ported node can keep.

<!-- /tabs -->

### Where its messages come from

In every language, the listener's `package.xml` is a standard ROS 2 manifest,
and its one `<depend>` names the message package the node uses:

```xml
<depend>std_msgs</depend>
```

That line is all you write for a message package. The build generates the
message code from your ROS 2 install and links it into the node: in Rust it
adds a dependency row to `Cargo.toml`, tagged `# nros-managed`, pointing at
the crate it generated under `generated/`; in C and C++, `find_package` finds
the generated code during the CMake configure. Removing the `<depend>` removes
the generated code from the node's build. A row in `Cargo.toml` without the
`# nros-managed` tag is yours and is never touched, so to override a
generated row, delete its tag.

Both nodes depend on `std_msgs`, and the build generates it once for the
workspace, not once per package. Chapter 5 adds a message package of your
own, which every node in the workspace can depend on the same way.

## See the bringup run both

```bash probe=320 track=installed variant=qemu
cat src/sensor_node_bringup/system.toml
```

`--to sensor_node_bringup` added a second `[[component]]` row, after the
talker's:

```toml
[[component]]
pkg = "sensor_node"
class = "sensor_node::Talker"
name = "sensor_node"

[[component]]
pkg = "monitor_node"
class = "monitor_node::Listener"
name = "monitor_node"
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pkg` | the node package: its `<name>` in `package.xml` |
| `class` | the class the package registers |
| `name` | the node's name at run time; chapter 7 renames one |

It also added `<exec_depend>monitor_node</exec_depend>` to the bringup's
`package.xml`, beside the talker's, so the bringup states every package it
runs, the way a ROS 2 bringup package does. To run a node package you
copied in from elsewhere, write both lines by hand.

The image table did not change. `[image.baremetal]` still names one board,
and it now builds both rows into its one program.

`nros graph` shows the same facts as an order: each package after the
packages it depends on, with the bringup last because it runs both nodes:

```bash probe=325 track=installed variant=qemu
nros graph
```

```text
monitor_node
sensor_node
sensor_node_bringup  <- monitor_node, sensor_node
```

The two node packages depend on nothing in the workspace. Neither one names
the other: the only thing they share is the topic name `/chatter` and its
type, `std_msgs/String`, which is all a ROS 2 publisher and subscriber ever
share.

Before you build, `nros check` catches the common mistakes in a workspace: a
row naming a package or class that does not exist, or a build file left in
the bringup:

```bash probe=330 track=installed variant=qemu
nros check --workspace .
```

```text
nros check: ok (workspace ., 3 pkg(s), 0 warning(s))
```

## Run both nodes

```bash probe=340 probe-run=900 track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run --expect 'I heard:'
```

```text probe-expect=340 variant=qemu
I heard: [Hello World: 1]
nros run: matched after
```

The run builds the new package, then boots the board. A Rust project's
console, trimmed:

```text
[INFO] monitor_node: [    0.039453] Subscriber created for topic: /chatter

Application setup complete — entering spin loop.
[INFO] sensor_node: [    1.025751] Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
[INFO] monitor_node: [    1.026723] I heard: [Hello World: 1]
nros run: matched after 3.2 s: [INFO] monitor_node: [    1.026723] I heard: [Hello World: 1]
```

This time the command names nothing to run. With nothing named, `nros run`
runs the workspace's only image, and `sensor_node_bringup:baremetal` is still
the only one.

`nros run sensor_node`, the spelling from chapter 1, no longer works. It
meant "the bringup whose only node is `sensor_node`", and the bringup now has
two, so it refuses and prints the full name that would work:

```text
nros run: `sensor_node` is a component of `sensor_node_bringup`, but never the only one, so it names no one image; name one:
  sensor_node_bringup:baremetal
```

`nros run sensor_node_bringup:baremetal` always works: it is the bringup and
the image, the name chapter 2's `--dry-run` printed. `nros run` never guesses
between several images; when a short name matches more than one, it lists the
full names instead.

To see which rule picked the image when nothing is named, add `--dry-run
--why` as in chapter 2. The `[provenance]` table's `image` line now says the
image was the workspace's only one, rather than the only image of the only
bringup that runs `sensor_node`. The same four spellings work for `nros build`
too, and chapter 9, which gives the project a second image, lists them in
the order they are tried.

The console also shows a warning from the listener's subscription: it asked
for a history of 10 messages, and this board's receive buffer holds 4. The
image granted 4 and told the ROS 2 graph so. Chapter 8 shows where that
number comes from and how to state the one you need.

## How two nodes share one board

Both nodes now run in one program, on a processor with one core and no
operating system. One executor runs every callback of both nodes, one at a
time: the talker's timer callback, then the listener's subscription callback
when the message arrives, then whatever is ready next. Nothing runs two
callbacks at once, so neither node needs a lock around its state.

The cost is that callbacks share the processor's time. A callback that waits,
spins or blocks holds up every other callback in the image, the other node's
included. Keep each callback short: read the message, update the state,
publish, return. Work that takes longer belongs in its own task on a board
with an RTOS, which [Pick a scheduling model](../guide/realtime/pick-a-scheduling-model.md)
covers, and [The execution model](../background/execution-model.md) explains
how the executor decides what runs next.

For the same reason, a node cannot make a blocking service call from inside
a callback: the executor is in the middle of running that callback, and the
reply could never be delivered. Chapter 6 shows where such calls go instead.

## What just happened

You turned a project of one node into a **workspace** of two, and the shape
did not change.

A nano-ros workspace is a directory of packages under `src/`, like a colcon
workspace. It has no root `Cargo.toml` or `CMakeLists.txt`, and no file that
lists its packages: `nros` finds each package by its `package.xml`. `nros
list` and `nros graph` show what it found. Each package keeps one role. A
node package holds one node and no board; a bringup holds the board, the
middleware and the list of nodes, and no code. Adding a node is therefore
always two edits: a package under `src/`, and a row in the bringup that runs
it. `nros new --to` makes both.

What differs from a colcon workspace is what a build produces. `colcon build`
builds each package into its own executables. `nros run` built the bringup's
one image, and both node packages went into it: one program for the board,
with one executor running both nodes' callbacks. Neither node package knows
the other is there. The talker would publish with no listener, and the
listener would wait with no talker, in this image or in two images on two
boards.

| ROS 2 | nano-ros |
|---|---|
| `ros2 pkg create` | `nros new <pkg>` inside the workspace; `--to <bringup>` adds its component row |
| `colcon build` | `nros build` (every image) or `nros build <image>` |
| `ros2 run <pkg> <exe>` | `nros run <node>`, when one bringup runs only that node |
| `ros2 launch <pkg> <file>` | `nros run <bringup>:<image>` |

[Organize a larger workspace](../guide/build/organize-a-larger-workspace.md)
covers what a workspace grows into: several bringups, shared packages, and
every field of the two roles.
